Painting is the foundational visual art form—the application of pigment via brush, palette knife, or other tool to a prepared surface, typically canvas, wood panel, or wall, to create image, pattern, or abstract composition. As one of humanity's oldest practices, painting bridges ritual, craft, and concept. It has been the dominant vehicle for Western visual art from the Renaissance onward. From representational portraiture to abstract color-field works, painting's flexibility—its capacity to capture light, emotion, and invisible ideas—has made it the medium through which countless movements from Impressionism to Surrealism have articulated their aesthetic and philosophical visions.

Humans have painted for tens of thousands of years. Cave paintings, ancient Egyptian tomb walls, medieval illuminated manuscripts—all testify to painting's deep antiquity. The Western tradition distinguishes painting from drawing and sculpture, though boundaries blur in contemporary practice.

Painting's unique advantage is its capacity to render light, texture, and translucency through layered pigment and glaze. Perspective and anatomical precision were painting's grand achievements in the Renaissance, enabling illusionistic depth. The invention of oil paint in the fifteenth century transformed the medium, allowing rich color, slow drying, and revisability.

Photography's invention in eighteen thirty-nine challenged painting's documentary function, liberating it toward abstraction and emotional expression. Painting remains economically and culturally central: original paintings command vast prices; museums organize around them. Digital and photographic media challenged painting's hegemony in the late twentieth century, yet painting persists as a foundational medium for artistic experimentation and expression.

Painting's material properties—the texture of brushstrokes, layering of pigment, interaction of color—cannot be fully replicated in reproduction and remain central to the medium's appeal. Each painting's surface carries the hand of the artist, and this physical presence across centuries still moves viewers in ways no photograph can replicate.
